To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the risk of thyroid cancer after radiation exposure increases with age and is higher for men than for women; 2) the risk of benign neoplasms increases with age and dose and is higher for women than for men; and 3) there is an increased risk of salivary-glands and parathyroid tumors after radiation exposure.

(1) radiation-induced cancers of the thyroid, parathyroid, and salivary glands occur decades after irradiation; (2) the clinical behavior of radiation-induced tumors of the head and neck region is similar to that of spontaneous tumors, and (3) patients with a history of neck irradiation require careful follow-up, including thyroid ultrasonography.

radiation-related thyroid cancers are more aggressive, and have a higher mortality rate compared to sporadic thyroid cancers, and that radiation-exposed patients with a history of thyroid cancer should be followed closely for the development of second primary cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term risks of radiation-related thyroid neoplasms in children and adolescents who were exposed to radiation in the head and/or neck region.

how to identify patients with a high risk for radiation-related neoplasms; how to evaluate these patients for thyroid, parathyroid, salivary gland and acoustic neuroma tumors; and how to manage these patients when they develop neoplasms.

the following questions: (a) What are the long-term risks for thyroid neoplasia in patients exposed to radiation in childhood? (b) How can we improve the clinical management of these patients, especially those who are at risk for thyroid cancer?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk of developing thyroid cancer after radiation exposure is increased, that this risk is related to the radiation dose, that the risk is higher in children than adults, and that this risk is increased in individuals with a family history of thyroid cancer or a history of radiation-induced thyroid nodules.
, in the presence of a history of radiation, the risk for thyroid cancer is higher, and that the risk for other neoplasias is also increased.
radiation exposure is associated with an increased risk for benign and malignant thyroid neoplasms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radiation-induced thyroid cancer is a rare event, but the risks of radiation-related neoplasms persist for decades after the exposure.
the thyroid cancer risk after radiation exposure continues to be significant, but the risks of other malignancies are not increased.
radiation exposure in the head and/or neck is a risk factor for the development of a wide variety of tumors, and that these risks are lifelong.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the clinical approach for radiation-related thyroid cancer is not different from other thyroid cancers, and that radiation-exposed patients should undergo regular screening to detect thyroid nodules and other neoplastic lesions.
the clinical management of thyroid cancer in a radiation-exposed patient is not different from the management of a patient without a history of radiation.

patients who were irradiated for benign conditions in childhood should have their thyroid function and thyroid structure evaluated at least every 3 years, and patients who were irradiation for a malignancy should have their thyroid and parathyroid function evaluated at least annually.
